title: Static Application Security Testing
summary: Static application security testing is the automated analysis of source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program, looking for patterns that indicate a security defect such as injection sinks reached by untrusted input, unsafe deserialisation, hard-coded cryptographic material or broken access control. Modern SAST engines combine pattern matching with dataflow and taint tracking, so a rule can follow a value from a source such as an HTTP parameter through assignments and function calls to a sink such as a database query. Because it works on the code itself, SAST can find defects on code paths that no test exercises, and it can be run on every commit, which makes it attractive as a pull-request gate. Its central limitation is the false positive rate: without whole-program context and runtime configuration, the engine cannot know whether a path is reachable or whether a sanitiser it cannot model already applies. For a practising engineer the discipline is therefore triage, not detection. A workable programme baselines existing findings, gates only on new high-confidence rules, tunes rules per repository, suppresses with expiring annotations, and assigns rule ownership so that noisy rules are fixed rather than ignored. The common failure modes are treating the raw finding count as a metric, enabling every rule at once and drowning the team, running SAST only on a nightly build so feedback arrives too late to change the design, and allowing unbounded suppressions that silently disable entire rule classes. Pairing SAST with dependency analysis, dynamic testing and code review covers the gaps each tool leaves.
objectives: You will be able to explain how taint tracking differs from pattern matching and what each approach can and cannot detect.
You will be able to configure a SAST scan as a pull-request gate that blocks on new high-confidence findings without failing on legacy debt.
You will be able to triage a SAST finding by tracing reachability and confirming whether a modelled sanitiser applies.
You will be able to write a suppression with a justification, an owner and an expiry date instead of a permanent ignore.
You will be able to explain why raw finding counts are a poor programme metric and what to measure instead.
You will be able to state which defect classes escape static analysis and which complementary testing technique covers each.
